question: Collect every numeric threshold across the library (dollar amounts, percentages, ratios, day counts): what it limits, who it applies to, and where it comes from.
author: planned by Claude Code (claude-fable-5-1)

program.title: Numeric threshold register
program.thesis: Every operative paragraph is gated on whether it states a real numeric threshold, then classified by number type, what it limits, who it binds, and how it bites; source falls out of doc, issuer and legal_force. Cross-document pairs then show where the same number recurs or diverges between statute, rules and guidance.

unit.rationale: A threshold lives in a single sentence or clause, so paragraphs are the right grain. Duplicate copies (Treasury print edition, scanned OCC 1184) and the academic DeFi paper are left out; purely contextual paragraphs, cost estimates and comment questions are filtered out to keep the set to operative text, at the cost of missing numbers mentioned only in background discussion.

doc_notes.note: Enacted US federal statute (2025) regulating payment stablecoins. Obligations mostly fall on permitted payment stablecoin issuers (bank subsidiaries, federal qualified issuers, state qualified issuers) and on federal and state regulators implementing it.

House-passed bill (not enacted) on digital commodity market structure. Covers digital commodity issuers, exchanges, brokers and dealers, and splits SEC and CFTC jurisdiction; Title VI restricts a Federal Reserve central bank digital currency.

Proposed (not final) Federal Reserve rule implementing the GENIUS Act for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers and banking organizations. Many numbers restate or implement GENIUS Act requirements.

Proposed (not final) Federal Reserve rule on application procedures for Board-supervised insured depository institutions seeking approval to issue payment stablecoins through a subsidiary under the GENIUS Act.
Proposed (not final) Treasury rule under the GENIUS Act on issuance, offer and sale of payment stablecoins (12 CFR Part 1523).

Treasury rule (12 CFR Part 1522) on forms and procedures for the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee's review of state certifications under the GENIUS Act. Applies mainly to state regulators and the Committee.
FinCEN interpretive guidance applying Bank Secrecy Act money services business rules to users, administrators and exchangers of virtual currency.
FinCEN interpretive guidance applying Bank Secrecy Act money transmission rules to business models involving convertible virtual currency (CVC).
New York DFS guidance for DFS-regulated issuers of US dollar-backed stablecoins, covering redeemability, reserves and attestations.
UK Financial Conduct Authority policy statement on financial promotion rules for cryptoassets. Applies to firms communicating or approving cryptoasset promotions to UK consumers; not US law.
Non-binding international Financial Stability Board recommendations addressed to national authorities on global stablecoin arrangements.
IRS notice treating virtual currency as property for US federal tax purposes. Applies to taxpayers and to payers with information reporting duties.
Non-binding White House working group policy report. Its numbers are mostly recommendations or descriptions of existing or proposed law, not rules of its own.
Non-binding SEC staff statement on when certain reserve-backed 'covered stablecoins' are not securities.

nodes.label: States numeric threshold
nodes.question: Does this paragraph state a specific numeric threshold that limits, triggers, or measures a legal or regulatory requirement, such as a dollar amount, a percentage, a ratio, or a count of days, months or years? Answer no if the only numbers are section or citation numbers, calendar dates, page numbers, list numbering, or descriptive statistics with no regulatory effect.
nodes.why: Cheap gate so the classifying questions only run on paragraphs that actually carry a threshold.

nodes.label: Number type
nodes.question: What kind of numeric threshold does this paragraph state? If it states several, pick the one most central to the requirement.

options.description: A monetary amount, e.g. $10,000,000,000 or $600
A percentage or basis-point figure, e.g. 20 percent
A ratio or multiple, e.g. 1 to 1 backing
A count of days, months or years, or a frequency such as monthly or within 180 days
A count of something else, e.g. number of persons, votes, transactions or units
A numeric threshold that fits none of the above

nodes.why: Separates the four kinds of number the question names.

nodes.label: What it limits
nodes.question: What does the numeric threshold in this paragraph limit or govern? Use scope_note for the document's subject if needed.

options.description: Reserve composition, backing ratio, or maturity of reserve assets
Capital, liquidity or other prudential financial requirements
A size or volume threshold that decides which regime, regulator or exemption applies (e.g. issuance or revenue above an amount)
How quickly or on what terms redemption or customer payout must happen
Frequency or deadline for reports, attestations, disclosures, notices or recordkeeping
Deadlines for applications, approvals, certifications or agency review decisions
Deadlines for agencies to issue rules or studies, effective dates, transition and comment periods
Ownership, voting, control or decentralization thresholds
Caps on offering size, sales, investment amounts, or per-transaction limits
Fine, penalty or imprisonment amounts
Tax or anti-money-laundering reporting or filing thresholds
Anything else

nodes.why: Answers 'what it limits' and gives the grouping used to pair like thresholds across documents.

nodes.label: Who it applies to
nodes.question: Who must comply with or is directly measured by the numeric threshold in this paragraph? Use scope_note to identify the covered parties if the paragraph does not name them.

options.description: Payment stablecoin issuers or stablecoin arrangements
Banks, depository institutions or their holding companies, other than as stablecoin issuers
Exchanges, brokers, dealers, custodians or other digital asset service providers
Issuers or developers of digital assets other than stablecoins, including blockchain projects
Money transmitters and other money services businesses
A federal regulator or other federal body that must act within the limit
State regulators or state regimes
Individual investors, consumers, customers or taxpayers
Another party, or not determinable

nodes.why: Answers 'who it applies to' in a form that can be counted and cross-tabulated.

nodes.label: How it bites
nodes.question: How does the numeric threshold in this paragraph operate?

options.description: A ceiling that must not be exceeded
A floor that must be met or exceeded
A time limit by which something must be done
A recurring interval, e.g. monthly or annually
Crossing the number changes which rules, regulator or status applies
An exact required value or a penalty amount
None of the above

nodes.why: Distinguishes caps, floors, deadlines and triggers, which read very differently in a register.

nodes.label: Borrowed from elsewhere
nodes.question: Does this paragraph attribute its numeric threshold to another law, rule or document (for example by restating or citing a statutory requirement) rather than setting the number itself?
nodes.why: Refines 'where it comes from': separates the original source of a number from documents that repeat it.

nodes.label: Legal force
nodes.question: What is the legal force of the numeric threshold as stated in this paragraph? Use scope_note to identify the type of document (statute, bill, proposed rule, final rule, guidance, report).

options.description: Set by an enacted statute or executive order that is in force
Set by a bill that has not been enacted
Set by a final, binding regulation or rule text
Set or proposed in a proposed rule, including proposed rule text and preamble proposals
Stated in agency guidance, interpretive letter, notice, ruling or staff statement
Recommended or discussed in a policy report or international standard, not binding
Only describes or summarizes a threshold existing elsewhere, or uses the number in an example or cost estimate

nodes.why: The question asks where each number comes from; legal force separates binding numbers from proposals and commentary.

nodes.label: Multiple thresholds
nodes.question: Does this paragraph state two or more distinct numeric thresholds (for example a dollar amount and a day count, or two different percentages) rather than a single one?
nodes.why: Flags rows where the single-choice classification hides additional numbers that a full register must capture.

nodes.label: Source of number
nodes.question: This paragraph attributes its numeric threshold to another law, rule or document. Which source does the number come from?

options.description: The GENIUS Act (payment stablecoin statute), including citations to its sections or 12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.
Another federal banking statute, such as the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, Bank Holding Company Act, National Bank Act or Federal Reserve Act
Federal securities or commodities law, such as the Securities Act, Exchange Act, Investment Company Act or Commodity Exchange Act
The Bank Secrecy Act or its implementing AML regulations
The Internal Revenue Code or Treasury tax regulations
Procedural or administrative law, such as the Administrative Procedure Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Regulatory Flexibility Act or Congressional Review Act
An existing federal agency regulation, such as capital rules in the CFR, not covered above
A state law or regulation, a foreign law, or an international standard
Another source, or the source is not identifiable

nodes.why: The 96 borrowed numbers have no follow-up; naming the source is the direct answer to 'where it comes from'.

nodes.label: Period length
nodes.question: How long is the time period that this paragraph sets as its central numeric threshold?
levels: Under 1 week (hours or up to 6 days)
nodes.why: Time periods are 239 of 376 rows; banding by length makes them comparable across documents.

nodes.label: Clock starts from
nodes.question: From what event does the time period in this paragraph start to run?

options.description: The date of enactment of an Act
The effective date of a law or rule, or publication in the Federal Register
Receipt or filing of an application, or the application being deemed complete
An agency decision, notice, order, denial or determination
An event at the regulated firm, such as a redemption request, crossing a size threshold, a breach, or a change in control
The end of a reporting period, such as month, quarter or fiscal year end
No start event; the period is a recurring interval or a duration such as a retention or holding period
Another start event or not stated

nodes.why: A day count means little without its start event; this turns each time period into a usable register entry.

nodes.label: Dollar size band
nodes.question: How large is the central dollar amount stated in this paragraph (convert foreign currency to an approximate US dollar equivalent)?
nodes.why: Separates small transaction and penalty amounts from the large issuer-size lines such as $10 billion and $50 billion.

nodes.label: Size trigger effect
nodes.question: What happens when the size threshold in this paragraph is crossed or met?

options.description: Supervision moves between regulators, for example from a State regime to a Federal regulator
Additional or stricter requirements apply, such as audited financial statements, capital or governance standards
An exemption, exclusion, safe harbor or lighter treatment applies below or above the line
The threshold determines eligibility for a status, license, registration or definition
The entity must stop, limit or wind down an activity
Another consequence or not stated

nodes.why: 46 size triggers say nothing yet about what the trigger does.

nodes.label: Agency action due
nodes.question: What must or may the government agency do within or by the numeric threshold in this paragraph?

options.description: Issue, propose or finalize regulations
Act on, approve, deny or deem complete an application or registration
Complete a study or submit a report to Congress or the President
Give notice, hold a hearing, or take an enforcement or appeal step
Review, certify or determine the status of a State or foreign regulatory regime
Receive public comments or run a consultation period
Another agency action, or the number is not a duty on the agency

nodes.why: Agencies account for 122 rows; this distinguishes rulemaking clocks from application and reporting clocks.

nodes.label: Other limit subject
nodes.question: The numeric threshold in this paragraph does not fit the main categories. What does it limit or govern?

options.description: Custody, segregation or safeguarding of customer assets
Marketing, promotions, cooling-off periods or other consumer protections
How long records must be kept
Officer, director or employee restrictions, such as conviction bars or post-employment limits
Transition periods, safe harbors, waivers or grandfathering
A number that is part of a definition, such as maturity limits defining an eligible asset
A burden, cost or impact estimate with no direct obligation
None of these

nodes.why: Breaks open the 37-row 'other' bucket of what is limited.

nodes.label: Other covered party
nodes.question: The party subject to the numeric threshold in this paragraph does not fit the main categories. Who is it?

options.description: Consumers, customers or stablecoin holders
Custodians, auditors, accountants or other service providers
Foreign issuers, foreign firms or foreign regulators
Officers, directors, controlling persons or other individuals
Congress, the President or other non-agency government bodies
Any person or the public generally
Not identifiable from the paragraph

nodes.why: Breaks open the 37-row 'other' bucket of who the threshold applies to.

nodes.label: Issuer class
nodes.question: Which class of stablecoin issuer is subject to the numeric threshold in this paragraph? Use scope_note if the paragraph does not name the class.

options.description: Permitted payment stablecoin issuers generally, with no distinction by charter or regulator
Federal qualified or OCC-licensed nonbank issuers
Subsidiaries of insured depository institutions or credit unions, or issuers supervised by the Board, FDIC or NCUA

Foreign payment stablecoin issuers
An applicant seeking approval to become an issuer, not yet approved
Another class of issuer, or the class cannot be determined

nodes.why: Stablecoin issuer holds 154 of 377 rows with no breakdown; 'who it applies to' needs the issuer class.

nodes.label: Missed deadline effect
nodes.question: What does this paragraph say happens if the deadline or time limit it states is not met?

options.description: The application or request is deemed approved or takes effect automatically
The request is deemed denied, or a status, approval or right lapses or is lost
A fine, penalty or enforcement action may follow
The period may be extended or tolled
The paragraph states no consequence for missing the deadline

nodes.why: Deadline is the largest function bucket (134) and has no follow-up; the consequence shows how hard each deadline really is.

nodes.label: What is reported
nodes.question: What report, disclosure or record does the numeric threshold in this paragraph govern?

options.description: Periodic publication or report of reserve composition or outstanding issuance
Accountant examination, attestation, certification, or audited financial statements
Regular reports or filings submitted to a regulator
Notice of a specific event such as an incident, change, breach or shortfall
Disclosure or notice given to customers, holders or investors
How long records must be kept
Another reporting or disclosure item

nodes.why: Reporting and disclosure holds 61 rows with no sub-type.

nodes.label: Application step
nodes.question: Which step in an application or review process does the numeric threshold in this paragraph govern?

options.description: Regulator determines whether the application is substantially complete, or requests more information
Regulator approves or denies the application
Regulator notifies or explains its decision to the applicant
Applicant supplies information, responds, or reapplies
Request for or conduct of a hearing, appeal or reconsideration
Commencing business, or expiry or conditions after approval
Another step

nodes.why: Application review is the largest 'what it limits' bucket (63) and has no breakdown by step.

nodes.label: Measured against
nodes.question: What quantity is the percentage or ratio in this paragraph measured against?

options.description: Value of stablecoins outstanding or issued, including reserve backing ratios such as 1 to 1
Total assets, reserve assets, or exposure to a single counterparty or asset class
Capital, operating expenses, or risk-weighted amounts
Ownership interests, voting securities, or token supply held or controlled
Revenue, transaction value, trading volume, or offering proceeds
An amount of tax, gain, or the base of a penalty
Another base, or not stated

nodes.why: A percentage or ratio is meaningless in a register without its denominator; these 61 rows have no follow-up.

nodes.label: Percentage size band
nodes.question: How large is the central percentage stated in this paragraph?
nodes.why: Time and dollar thresholds have magnitude bands; percentages do not.

nodes.label: How numbers relate
nodes.question: This paragraph states two or more numeric thresholds. How do they relate to each other?

options.description: Tiers or steps of the same measure, such as different amounts for different sizes or classes
A base period or amount plus an extension, cap or outer limit
An amount or percentage paired with the time period over which it is measured or must be met
Alternative tests, where either one applies (greater of, lesser of, or)
Successive deadlines for different steps in one process
Separate thresholds for unrelated requirements

nodes.why: The 60 multi-threshold paragraphs are recorded under a single central number; this shows what the register flattens.

nodes.label: Other clock start
nodes.question: The time period in this paragraph does not start from a standard event. What best describes how it runs?

options.description: Runs from a request or transaction by a customer or holder, such as a redemption request
A term, holding period, lookback, retention or maturity length with no triggering event
Measured to or from a fixed calendar date
Runs from receipt of a notice, or from discovery of a fact
The paragraph does not say when the period starts

nodes.why: 'Other' is the second-largest clock-start bucket (49).

nodes.label: Basis for number
nodes.question: This paragraph sets its numeric threshold without attributing it to another law. What basis, if any, does it give for the number chosen?

options.description: The number is stated as a requirement with no explanation
The agency explains why it chose the number, based on its own judgment, data or experience
The number is modeled on or aligned with an existing regime, industry practice or standard, without being attributed to it as the legal source
The paragraph asks for comment on the number or offers alternatives to it
The number is an example or illustration, not a requirement

nodes.why: 281 rows are marked as not borrowed with nothing on where the number comes from; this fills the 'where it comes from' gap for numbers that originate in the document.

nodes.label: Regulator can adjust
nodes.question: Does this paragraph allow a regulator or other authority to change, waive, extend or set a different value for the numeric threshold it states?
nodes.why: Separates fixed numbers from those a regulator can move, which matters for every entry in the register.

nodes.label: Time counting unit
nodes.question: In what unit is the central time period in this paragraph expressed?

options.description: Expressed in hours
Expressed in business or working days
Expressed in days, either stated as calendar days or with no qualifier
Expressed in weeks, months or quarters
Expressed in years
Another unit or not clear

nodes.why: Time periods are 242 of 377 thresholds. The counting unit, especially business versus calendar days, is needed to state each one exactly.

nodes.label: How number is borrowed
nodes.question: This paragraph attributes its numeric threshold to another law, rule or document. How does it use that source's number?

options.description: Restates or summarizes the source's number unchanged
Adopts the source's number and adds operational detail such as how to calculate or measure it
Sets a stricter or additional number on top of the source's number
Sets a looser number or an exemption relative to the source
Points to the source without restating the number's content
Cannot tell from the paragraph

nodes.why: There are 96 borrowed numbers, 70 of them from the GENIUS Act. Knowing whether they are duplicates of the statutory number or modified versions is essential for a deduplicated register with provenance.

nodes.label: Adjustment mechanism
nodes.question: This paragraph lets an authority change, waive, extend or set a different value for its numeric threshold. By what mechanism?

options.description: The authority may extend a deadline or time period
The authority may waive the threshold or exempt a party from it
The authority may set or revise the number by rulemaking or order
The authority may impose a stricter or higher number on a specific firm
The number adjusts automatically, for example for inflation
Another mechanism or not clear

nodes.why: The 34 adjustable thresholds have no follow-up. The mechanism shows how firm each number actually is.

nodes.label: Reserve aspect
nodes.question: Which aspect of stablecoin reserves or backing does the numeric threshold in this paragraph govern?

options.description: The overall ratio of reserves to outstanding stablecoins, such as one-to-one backing
The maximum remaining maturity or term of eligible reserve assets, such as Treasury bills of 93 days or less
A cap on the share of reserves held in one asset type, counterparty or institution
A minimum share of reserves in cash, deposits or same-day liquid assets
Terms of repurchase or reverse repurchase agreements, including overcollateralization or tenor
Haircuts, buffers or valuation frequency for reserve assets
Another reserve aspect

nodes.why: The reserves branch (29 rows) has no follow-up, and it is the core substantive limit in the stablecoin documents.

nodes.label: Capital/liquidity aspect
nodes.question: Which capital or liquidity measure does the numeric threshold in this paragraph govern?

options.description: A fixed minimum dollar amount of capital
Capital as a ratio or percentage of assets, exposures or outstanding stablecoins
Capital or liquid assets sized to a number of months of operating expenses
A liquidity buffer or coverage requirement
A risk weight, deduction or calculation parameter used in computing capital
Operational risk capital or loss-data parameters
Another capital or liquidity measure

nodes.why: The capital and liquidity branch (20 rows) has no follow-up. The measure governed is needed to say what each number limits.

nodes.label: Ownership threshold effect
nodes.question: What does the ownership or control threshold in this paragraph determine?

options.description: Defines when a person controls an entity or is an affiliate or related person
Tests whether a blockchain system or digital asset is decentralized or mature, such as a cap on holdings or voting power
Triggers a requirement for regulatory approval or notice of an acquisition or change in control
Triggers disclosure of holders or insiders above a stake
Restricts how much insiders or holders may sell or hold
Another effect

nodes.label: Penalty form
nodes.question: What form does the numeric penalty in this paragraph take?

options.description: A civil money penalty per day of violation
A civil money penalty per violation or a fixed cap
A criminal fine
A term of imprisonment
A time-limited bar, suspension or prohibition on a person or firm
A tax penalty or addition to tax
Another form

nodes.label: Rule timing kind
nodes.question: What kind of rulemaking or effectiveness timing does the numeric threshold in this paragraph set?

options.description: A deadline for an agency to propose or finalize rules
When a statute, rule or provision takes effect
A transition, phase-in, grace or safe-harbor period for regulated parties
The length of a public comment period
When a provision or authority expires
A deadline for a study or report tied to rulemaking
Another kind

nodes.why: The rulemaking and effective-date branch (55 rows) mixes agency deadlines with transition periods that bind firms.

nodes.label: Other reported item
nodes.question: The report, disclosure or record governed by the numeric threshold in this paragraph did not fit the main categories. What is it?

Risk warnings, cooling-off periods or financial promotion content

nodes.label: Other agency action

Granting a waiver, exemption or extension
Consulting, coordinating or sharing information with another authority

nodes.label: Role of statement
nodes.question: In what capacity does this paragraph state its numeric threshold? Use scope_note to identify the document type.

options.description: Operative statutory, bill or regulatory text that itself imposes the number as a requirement
Preamble, summary or discussion that describes or explains a requirement set elsewhere in the same document or in another law
A question or request for comment about whether the number is appropriate or what it should be
A worked example, hypothetical or illustration using the number
An estimate of costs, burden hours, or number of affected entities, not a requirement
Background, history or description of market facts or other regimes with no requirement imposed here
None of the above

nodes.why: Proposed rules account for 133 rows and probably mix regulatory text with preamble restatements. A register should separate the paragraph that sets a number from the ones that discuss it, and expose false positives such as estimates.

views.why: Shows whether statutes, proposed rules and guidance explain, borrow by analogy, or simply state their numbers

views.title: What happens when a deadline is missed
views.why: Shows how many deadlines carry a stated consequence such as deemed approval or a penalty, and how many carry none

views.title: How borrowed numbers are used, by legal force
views.why: Shows whether rules and guidance merely repeat statutory numbers or tighten and elaborate on them, separating duplicate entries from genuinely new ones.

views.title: What reserve thresholds govern
views.why: Breaks the reserves branch into backing ratio, maturity, concentration and liquidity limits.

views.title: Time counting unit by what the period limits
views.why: Shows where business-day, calendar-day, month and year clocks are used across redemption, application, reporting and rulemaking deadlines.

views.title: Operative vs. explanatory thresholds by legal force
views.why: Shows how many thresholds are actually set in operative text and how many are preamble restatements, questions or estimates, for each document type.

views.title: Exact time periods by who they bind
views.why: Shows which day counts (30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 270, 1 year) recur and whether they bind agencies or regulated firms.

views.title: Operative thresholds by administering authority
views.why: Shows which regulator is responsible for the thresholds that are actually imposed, which answers where the numbers come from.

followups.rationale: The new layers pin down where each number comes from (legal force and the source of borrowed numbers), size the two dominant number types (time periods and dollar amounts), and break open the largest buckets: time periods, federal-agency deadlines, size triggers and the two 'other' catch-alls.

The new layers split the largest unrefined buckets (stablecoin issuers, deadlines, reporting, application review, percentages and ratios, multi-threshold paragraphs, clock-start 'other') and add where a non-borrowed number comes from and whether a regulator can change it. Together they sharpen all three parts of the register: what each number limits, who it binds, and its origin.

The new layers break open the largest catch-alls (other reports, other agency actions) and add first follow-ups to branches that had none: reserves, capital, ownership, penalties, rulemaking timing and adjustable numbers. They also record how time periods are counted and whether borrowed numbers are restated exactly or tightened, so each register entry says more precisely what the number limits and where it comes from.

The new layers separate operative thresholds from preamble, examples and estimates, name the authority behind each number, and pin down recurring values (exact day counts, the $10 billion line, what the dollar figure measures). They also fill untouched branches: non-size triggers, firm-side deadlines, minimum/maximum measurement, second numbers in multi-threshold paragraphs, and what implementing rules add to statutory numbers.
